name: Jade Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Theo and I lease twenty-two hectares on the edge of town: outdoor pigs, about two hundred laying hens, and vegetables in the fields and two polytunnels. We sell most of it through a weekly veg box to about a hundred and forty households. My day starts with the pigs and the hens, then I'm picking and packing, and by four I'm in the van doing the box round while an app tells me the best route.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned an app. How much do you use that kind of thing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask an AI assistant to plan the planting so we don't get forty kilos of courgettes in one week, and it writes the newsletter that goes out with the boxes. Money's the hard part: we borrowed for the polytunnels two years ago, and Theo's part-time wage at the hardware store covers the mortgage, so there's almost nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like 'turns out the robot isn't coming to weed my carrots after all'. Most of my customers would laugh, they think I'm a bit of a gadget nerd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for us. The tools I use now would keep getting a bit better, the boxes keep selling, and the big change I was half hoping for, cheap help with the hard graft, just doesn't come. We'd carry on as we are, slightly tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for planning and the newsletter and try a couple more tools for the accounts. I'd keep going with the boxes and try to get up to a hundred and sixty customers by next spring. That's the number where we'd finally have a bit of slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. It's like ordering a new tool and getting a slightly sharper version of the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hard graft you'd hoped a machine would take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding, all of it. In June I'm on my knees in the carrot beds for three hours a day and my back is forty-three going on seventy. There are little weeding robots already, but they cost more than our van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find those extra twenty customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly word of mouth, and I'd get the AI to help me write a proper offer for the new estate on Ridgeway Road. People there have just moved in and don't know a farm is five minutes away.

S0.say: She'd joke online that the robot isn't coming to weed her carrots after all. Her customers already see her as a bit of a gadget fan.
S0.think: It's fine for the farm, since the tools she uses keep improving and the boxes keep selling. But the cheap help with heavy work she was hoping for never arrives.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for planning and the newsletter and tries a few more tools for the accounts. Aims to grow the veg box scheme from 140 to 160 customers by next spring by marketing to a new housing estate.
S0.feel: Calm but a little flat, like getting a slightly sharper version of an old tool.
S0.quote: In June I'm on my knees in the carrot beds for three hours a day and my back is forty-three going on seventy.
S0.fieldNote: She is the rare farmer who'd be disappointed by AI hype collapsing. Her interest is practical: she wants a machine to take the weeding off her back. The customer target of 160 shows she thinks in clear numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small farms if we're smart about it, and bad news if we let the big companies own all the machines. I'd be posting about sharing robots between farms, like the old machinery rings where neighbours shared a combine. I'd want the government to back that with grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it, at least at first. A weeding robot and a packing helper would let me grow without hiring, and my customers buy from me because they know me, not because I'm the cheapest. The danger is if the supermarkets get so cheap that people stop caring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find three or four other small growers and go halves on a weeding robot, maybe through a lease, because we can't buy one. I'd use AI to run the shared booking calendar. And I'd start doing a cooking class at the farm once a month, as a side income that a robot can't really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A little uneasy about the money, because leasing anything is a risk when you've got nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the other growers you'd ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who does salad leaves past the river, and the two lads at the orchard, who are younger than me and even keener on gadgets. We already swap seedlings and gossip. Asking them to share a robot is just the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger is supermarkets getting cheaper. How would you know it was happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cancellations. Right now we lose two or three boxes a month and gain four or five. If it flipped round for three months running, I'd know, and I'd be worried.

S1.say: This is good for small farms if they're smart, and bad if big companies own all the machines. She'd promote sharing robots between farms, backed by government grants.
S1.think: She expects to do well at first, because a weeding robot would let her grow without hiring, and customers buy from her because they know her. Her worry is supermarkets becoming so cheap that people stop caring where food comes from.
S1.do: Leases a shared weeding robot with three or four local growers and uses AI to run the booking calendar. Starts a monthly cooking class at the farm as extra income.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some unease about taking on a lease with nothing in the bank.
S1.quote: Asking them to share a robot is just the next step.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opening rather than a threat, and her answer is collective: shared machines, not bigger debt. She has a clear early-warning sign in the box cancellation rate. The cooking class idea shows she's already looking for work machines can't easily copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of the big systems, or at least strong rules, and we needed them yesterday. I'd be posting about a robot tax and a basic income. People would expect me to be cheering because I love the tech, and I'd surprise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast for someone with no savings. The big farms would have robots doing everything in months, food prices drop, and my customers, a lot of whom are teachers and office workers, lose their jobs too and cancel the box. It's not my job I'd lose first, it's my customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut the lease plan and anything that isn't feed, seed and the mortgage. I'd use AI to set up a lower-cost box and a pay-what-you-can option to hold on to people. I'd join with the other small growers to lobby the council for local food contracts, schools and the hospital, because public buyers don't vanish overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I've always been the one telling everyone the future's exciting, and this is the version where I'd feel stupid for saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mei and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei's twelve and she reads the news, so she'd ask me straight if we're going to be okay. I'd tell her we'd still have food, because we grow it, and that's true. I wouldn't tell her about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You love new tools. Is there any part of this that still excites you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot could do my weeding for nearly nothing, yes, a little part of me would be thrilled. But it doesn't help if nobody can afford to buy what I grow. That's the bit people who love the tech forget.

S2.say: This shows why public ownership or strong rules on the big AI systems were needed yesterday. She'd post about a robot tax and a basic income, surprising people who expect her to cheer.
S2.think: Two years is too fast for someone with no savings, and her customers, many of them teachers and office workers, would lose jobs and cancel boxes. She'd lose customers before she lost her job.
S2.do: Drops the robot lease and cuts everything except feed, seed and the mortgage. Sets up a cheaper box and pay-what-you-can option with AI, and lobbies the council with other growers for school and hospital food contracts.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and embarrassed that she's always told people the future is exciting.
S2.quote: It's not my job I'd lose first, it's my customers.
S2.fieldNote: Her fear isn't about robots replacing her, it's about the people who buy from her losing their income. She turns quickly to public buyers like schools and the hospital, which shows good instincts under pressure. The gap between her public image as a tech fan and her private alarm is striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build local food systems that don't depend on everyone having a job. Councils buying from local farms, shared robots, community-owned land. I'd say it loudly and I'd probably start a group for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to get the robots in on my terms before the big farms make me irrelevant. If I can get my costs right down and lock in the school contracts, I think we'd survive. Not get rich, survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the shared robot lease after all, and use the savings to pay off the polytunnel loan early. I'd go after a contract to supply the primary school on Ridgeway Road. And I'd start the growers' group properly, with meetings and a shared website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious that gets me up early. I'd have a plan and a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two years and five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm defending. Five years, I'm building. I need about two growing seasons to try something, fail and try again, and five years gives me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Theo's job at the hardware store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't have an answer for. Self-checkouts are already in, and an AI that knows where every screw is will finish off what's left. He might end up working on the farm full-time, which we'd have to make pay.

S3.say: Five years is enough to build local food systems that don't rely on everyone having a job. She'd push for council buying from local farms, shared robots and community land, and probably start a group.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to bring in robots on her own terms before big farms make her irrelevant. With low costs and school contracts, she thinks the farm would survive but not thrive.
S3.do: Takes up the shared robot lease and uses the savings to pay off the polytunnel loan early. Bids to supply the primary school and formally starts a local growers' group.
S3.feel: Anxious in a way that gets her up early, because she has a plan and a deadline.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm defending. Five years, I'm building.
S3.fieldNote: The difference between scenarios is clear in her own words: two seasons of trial and error is what she needs. She is less sure about her partner's job than her own, which she admits honestly. She combines automating her own work with organising other growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Farmers like me should be helping design the robots and the rules, not just reacting. I'd be online saying it and I'd be at every planning meeting the council held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be okay. In ten years I could turn the farm into something robots help with, and the bit people pay for is the farm itself, the visits, the classes, knowing who grew it. I'd be fifty-three and a bit wiser, hopefully with the loan gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in the shared robots in the first couple of years and grow the cooking classes into school visits and farm days. I'd do an online course in small-farm robotics so I can fix things myself. And I'd sit down with Mei about what she wants to study, because she'll be choosing just as it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly hopeful. Like the first warm day in March when you know you're early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the farm's value would be the visits and knowing who grew it. What if a robot grows it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm the person who chose the seeds and runs the place and says hello. People still go to a restaurant even though they could cook. I'm betting on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mei to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where she's with people. Nursing, teaching, I don't mind. Not something that's all screens, funnily enough, even though I'm the one always on a screen.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if it's used well, and farmers should help design the robots and the rules rather than just react. She'd say it online and at council planning meetings.
S4.think: She thinks they'd be okay, turning the farm into a place robots help run while people pay for visits, classes and knowing who grew the food. She hopes to be 53 with the loan cleared.
S4.do: Brings in shared robots in the first couple of years and grows cooking classes into school visits and farm days. Takes an online course in small-farm robotics and talks with her daughter about what to study.
S4.feel: Uneasy at the edges but mostly hopeful, like an early warm day in March.
S4.quote: People still go to a restaurant even though they could cook.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she sees the farm becoming a place people visit rather than just a food producer. She's surprisingly firm that her daughter should avoid screen-based work, which runs against her own habits. Thin savings still keep a little unease in the picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because it's my customers who'd go under, and I can't sell veg boxes to people with no wages. What would help is public money going into local food, like schools and hospitals buying from farms nearby, and a basic income so people can still buy food.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd eat. Everyone talks about jobs. I'd want to know who owns the farms when the robots do the work, because whoever owns the food owns a lot more than food.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the food owns a lot more than food.
portrait: Jade Zhang is 43 and leases a small farm with her partner Theo, raising pigs, hens and vegetables for a veg box scheme of about 140 households, with a polytunnel loan and almost no savings. She uses AI every day and loves new tools, but her politics lean left and she wants machines shared and food systems publicly backed. In the milder scenarios she is calm, even excited, and plans to share a weeding robot with neighbours. With AGI in two years she is alarmed, not for her own job but because her customers would lose theirs. With five or ten years she shifts from defending to building, turning the farm into a place for visits, classes and school supply.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her customers would lose their wages and stop buying veg boxes.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for local food, such as schools and hospitals buying from nearby farms, and a basic income so people can still afford food.
